Decided on : 25.09.2026
K. M. S. DISSANAYAKE, J.
Instant application in revision has been preferred to this Court by the 2nd
Respondent-Petitioner seeking inter-alia, to set aside the order dated
28.04.2026, made in the exercise of the special jurisdiction vested in him by
Section 9 of the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction Act No. 10 of
2001 (hereinafter called and referred to as “the Act”) by the learned High Court
Judge of the Western Province holden in Colombo (hereinafter called and
referred to as “the learned High Court Judge”) in an action styled “Special
Child Abduction HC 01/2025” a certified copy of which was annexed to the
petition furnished to this Court by Petitioner marked as ‘A10’ (hereinafter
called and referred to as ‘the HC order”) (Vide- prayer ‘C’ of the petition) and
to uphold and sustain the preliminary objection so raised by the 2nd
Respondent-Petitioner and dismiss the Petitioner-Respondent’s application
dated 03.10.2025 in-limine (Vide- prayer ‘D’ of the petition), or in the
alternative to prayer ‘C’ and ‘D’, to direct the learned High Court Judge to
determine the said preliminary objection and adduce reasons therefor (Vide-
prayer ‘E’ of the petition).
Instant application in revision was on the other hand, vehemently, opposed
by both the Petitioner-Respondent as well as the 1st Respondent-Respondent
on the grounds enumerated in their respective statement of objections.
The facts material to the instant application in revision may be briefly, set out
below.
The Petitioner-Respondent being the holder of the office of the Secretary
to the Ministry of Justice and by virtue of the said office the Petitioner-
Respondent being the Central Authority within the meaning of section 4 of
Page 5 of 19
the Act; that, by virtue of the powers vested in her under and in terms of
section 9 of the Act as the Central Authority, the Petitioner-Respondent had
in her application dated 03.10.2025, made an application to the High Court
of the Western Province holden in Colombo (hereinafter called and referred to
as “the High Court of the Province”) praying inter-alia, for an interlocutory
order in terms of Sec 377(b) of the Civil Procedure Code in respect of the 2nd
Respondent-Petitioner (Vide- prayer ‘b’ of the petition); a declaration declaring
that the 2nd Respondent-Petitioner has contravened the provisions of Section
3 of the Act (Vide- prayer ‘d’ of the petition); an order for the return of the
child named in the petition (hereinafter called and referred to as “the child”)
to her habitual residence in Canada (Vide- prayer ‘e’ of the petition); together
with an interim order restraining the 2nd Respondent-Petitioner from taking
the child beyond the territorial limits of Sri Lanka until the final determination
of this matter (Vide-prayer ‘c’ of the petition); that, the 2nd Respondent-
Petitioner who had in his statement of objections, raised an array of
preliminary objections as to the maintainability of the application made to
the High Court of the Province by the Petitioner-Respondent in his statement
of objections, had raised a further preliminary objection as to the
maintainability of the application on 23.02.2026 on the premise, that the
affidavit dated 02.10.2025 which was filed in support of the application dated
03.10.2025, was defective in as much as it had been attested by a
Commissioner for Oaths who was an employee of the Central Authority, and
therefore had come within the prohibition embodied in the proviso to Section
12(2) of the Oaths Ordinance of No 09 of 1895 as amended (hereinafter called
and referred to as “the Oaths Ordinance”), and invited the Court to hear and
determine it in the first instance; and that, the learned High Court Judge who
heard the preliminary objection on the strength of the written submissions
furnished to Court by all the parties, had in the HC order, directed the
Petitioner-Respondent to furnish to Court a duly, attested affidavit in place of
the affidavit already furnished to the Court by the Petitioner-Respondent
along with her application. It is this order (HC order) that the 2nd Respondent-
Petitioner now, seeks to revise and set aside in the instant application in
revision on the purported exceptional circumstances urged in paragraph 13
Page 6 of 19
(a) to (h) of the petition which may be reproduced verbatim the same as
follows;
“a) The Impugned Order is ex facie bad in law in that the learned High
Court Judge failed to rule on or make any determination in respect of
the Preliminary Objection duly raised before the Court.
b) The Impugned Order is bad in law in that the learned High Court
Judge gave no reasons whatsoever for his decision and failed to deal
with the submissions presented to His Honor in support of the
Preliminary Objection.
c) The Impugned Order is contrary to and inconsistent with the binding
precedent of the Supreme Court of Sri Lanka in Case Land Reform
Commission v. Kandy Plantations Ltd - SC/HCCA/LA/35/2020;
SCM 06.06.2024, which was placed before His Honor for adjudication.
d) The learned High Court Judge failed to appreciate that once a
supporting affidavit is found to be bad in law, that defect goes to the
very root of the application itself and renders the entire application
invalid. As decided by the Supreme Court in the said case which His
Honor himself referred to in the Impugned Order - such a fatal defect
cannot be rectified by the tendering of a fresh affidavit, and that
determination constitutes binding precedent.
e) The Impugned Order is contrary to the express mandatory provisions
of Section 12(2) of the Oaths and Affirmations Ordinance No. 9 of 1895
and the clear and unambiguous rulings of the Supreme Court of Sri
Lanka on the said provision. The learned High Court Judge, in
overruling the Preliminary Objection, failed to appreciate and apply the
correct legal test. The order is, therefore, on its face, illegal.
f) The Impugned Order permits the Respondent who filed a supporting
affidavit that is a nullity in law - to cure that fundamental and incurable
defect by the mere expedient of filing a fresh affidavit. A defect of this
Page 7 of 19
nature goes to the very root of the application and strikes at its
evidentiary foundation. To permit its cure at this stage is directly
contrary to binding Supreme Court authority and shocks the
conscience of the Court.
g) The learned High Court Judge made the Impugned Order without
setting out any reasons therefor. An order made without reasons,
particularly one overruling a preliminary objection founded on a clear
and binding line of Supreme Court authority, is not a judicial
determination in any meaningful sense. The Impugned Order is, on that
basis, a nullity.
h) The Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction Act No. 10 of 2001
does not confer any right of appeal against an interlocutory order made
thereunder. There is accordingly no appellate remedy available to the
Petitioner. The revisionary jurisdiction of Your Lordship's Court is the
sole and only recourse, and its invocation is both necessary and
appropriate in the circumstances.”
The Petitioner-Respondent on the other hand, seeks to resist the instant
application in revision on the grounds urged in paragraph 5 of her statement
of objections which may be, re-produced verbatim the same as follows;
“a. By the Impugned Order dated 28th April 2026 marked as "A10" with
the Petition, the Learned High Court Judge, in part, agreed with the
Petitioner that the Affidavit is faulty and in part agreed with the
Respondent that it is a curable defect and could be rectified by the
Respondent filing a fresh Affidavit;
b. The said Order of the Learned High Court Judge is valid in law and
should be upheld also in view of any purported defect in the affidavit
dated 3rd October 2025 would not defeat the application made by the
Respondent under and in terms of the Child Abduction Act for the
following reasons and any other reason that the Counsel for the
Respondent may submit to Your Lordships during these proceedings:
Page 8 of 19
i. The Act provides in Section 9 (2) that the proceedings
before the High Court should be by way of summary
procedure in terms of the Civil Procedure Code (as
amended);
ii. In terms of Chapter XXIV of the Civil Procedure Code and
in particular, Section 373, filing of a Petition is sufficient to
institute proceedings by way of Summary Procedure.
iii. Section 376 provides that affidavits and/or other material
could be attached to the petition only so far as it is
convenient to do so, which confirms that it is not
mandatory to have an affidavit accompany the Petition so
filed.
iv. The contents of the affidavit/nature of evidence admitted
through the said affidavit falls within the exception to
Section 181 of the Civil Procedure Code, and thus permit
evidence other than direct evidence.
v. The matters which the High Court is called upon to
consider in considering the interlocutory order prayed for
under Section 377 (b) and the travel restriction in respect
of the Petitioner and the child are contained in the
Application of the 1st Respondent-Respondent (found at
pages 530-532 of the case record marked as 'A' attached to
the Petition). The said application is admissible as evidence
in terms of Section 15 of the Child Abduction Act. Thus,
any purported defect in the Affidavit by which the said
application was referred cannot be construed as
invalidating the proceedings filed before the High Court.”
Apart from the preliminary objection raised in paragraph 1 of the statement
of objections as to the maintainability of the instant application in revision,
the 1st Respondent-Respondent seeks to resist the instant application in
Page 9 of 19
revision on the grounds urged in paragraph 14 (a),(b) and (c) of her statement
of objections which may be, re-produced verbatim the same as follows;
a) The affidavit has been duly attested by the Assistant Secretary (Legal)
to the Ministry of Justice in her capacity as a Justice of the Peace;
b) Section 12 and the proviso to Section 12(2) of the Oaths Ordinance
only applies to the Commissioners for Oaths and is not applicable to a
Justice of the Peace;
c) In any event, the Assistant Secretary (Legal) to the Ministry of Justice
is not an "attorney-at-law to any of the parties" and does not have a
personal "interest" on the return of the minor child to the habitual
residence, and as such, the said proviso does not apply in law.”
It is in this context, I would think it expedient at this juncture to carefully,
examine the brief HC order.
The operative part of the HC order in its literal context, reads thus;
“අධිකරණයේදී යෙපාර්ශවය විසින් ඉදිරිපත් කරන ලෙ කරුණු සළකා බැලීයෙන් අනතුරුව
යෙෙ යේඛනයේ අවස්ථා සලකා බලා යපත්සම්කරු විසින් විධිෙත් යපත්සෙක් ඉදිරිපත් කිරීෙට
ඉඩදීෙ උචිත බව යපනී යන යෙයින් සති යෙකක කාලයක් තුළ යළි විධිෙත්ෙ අත්සන් තබන ලෙ
දිවුරුම් ප්‍රකාශයක් යගානු කිරීෙට නියයෝග කරමි.”
However, a cursory glance of the operative part of the brief HC order as quoted
above, does not explicitly, show as to whether the learned High Court Judge
had upheld or rejected the preliminary objection so raised by the 2nd
Respondent-Petitioner. However, upon a careful and close scrutiny of the brief
HC order, the irresistible inference that one may reasonably, draw from the
specific direction made by the learned High Court Judge on the Petitioner-
Respondent that she should furnish to Court a duly, attested affidavit in place
of the affidavit already furnished to the Court by the Petitioner-Respondent
along with her application is that he had thereby, implicitly, upheld the
preliminary objection so raised by the 2nd Respondent-Petitioner as to the
maintainability of the application of the Petitioner-Respondent on the said
premise that, the affidavit dated 02.10.2025 which was filed in support of the
Page 10 of 19
application dated 03.10.2025, was defective in as much as it had been
attested by a Commissioner for Oaths who was an employee of the Central
Authority, and therefore had come within the prohibition embodied in the
proviso to Section 12(2) of the Oaths Ordinance of No 09 of 1895 as amended
(hereinafter called and referred to as “the Oaths Ordinance”).
It is significant to observe that the Petitioner-Respondent in paragraph 5 (a)
and (b) of the statement of objections filed before this Court in resisting the
instant application in revision, had clearly, and unequivocally, admitted that
it was so when she stated therein, that, the Learned High Court Judge had in
the HC Order, agreed in part with the 2nd Respondent-Petitioner that the
Affidavit is faulty while agreeing in part with the Petitioner-Respondent that
the defect was curable and thus it could be rectified by the Petitioner-
Respondent in furnishing a fresh Affidavit duly attested and therefore,
purported defect in the affidavit dated 03.10.2025 would not defeat the
application made by the Petitioner-Respondent under and in terms of the
Child Abduction Act, hence, the HC order is valid in law and should thus, be
upheld.
Furthermore, the fact that the 1st Respondent-Respondent had not taken any
step to canvass the HC order, clearly, and unequivocally, shows that she too,
had admitted the correctness of the said findings of the learned High Court
Judge.
Moreover, the 2nd Respondent-Petitioner too, had admitted that it was so, in
view of the matters adverted to by him in paragraphs 6 and 7 of the synopsis
of submissions dated 01.09.2026, that, the Respondents are barred and
estopped from advancing the aforesaid contentions for the reasons that the
Learned High Court Judge, having heard the preliminary objection raised by
the Petitioner and the oral and written submissions made on behalf of all
parties, agreed, in part, with the Petitioner that the Affidavit was "faulty"; and
that the Petitioner-Respondent in paragraph 5 of the Statement of Objections,
has conceded that the order of the learned High Court Judge is correct in
part, by agreeing with the Petitioner that the Affidavit is faulty; and that,
Page 11 of 19
critically, the Respondent has not filed any appeal or application for revision
against the finding that the Affidavit is defective and thus, by deliberately
choosing not to challenge that finding before an appropriate Court, the
Respondent has unequivocally accepted and acquiesced in the finding that
the Affidavit is indeed defective.
Hence, the Petitioner-Respondent and the 1st Respondent-Respondent had
clearly, and unequivocally, admitted in no uncertain terms that the learned
High Court Judge, having heard the preliminary objection raised by the
Petitioner and the oral and written submissions made on behalf of all parties,
agreed, in part, with the 2nd Respondent-Petitioner that the Affidavit was
"faulty".
In the circumstances, both the Petitioner-Respondent as well as the 1st
Respondent-Respondent are now, debarred and estopped in law from re-
agitating the validity and/or legal soundness of the said findings before this
Court as rightly, contended by the learned President’s Counsel for the 2nd
Respondent-Petitioner.
However, it is regrettable to observe, that, both the Petitioner-Respondent and
the 1st Respondent-Respondent had nonetheless, made a futile attempt in the
course of the argument before us to re-agitate the same issue in respect of
which a clear and definite finding had admittedly, been so reached by the
learned High Court Judge as enumerated above, by contending that the
prohibition enumerated in proviso to section 12(2) of the Oaths Ordinance
would not be applicable to the affidavit in question for; it had been attested
by a Justice of the Peace and not a Commissioner for Oaths, which clearly,
and unequivocally, shows that the Petitioner-Respondent and the 1st
Respondent-Respondent had thus, attempted to contend that the findings of
the learned High Court Judge as enumerated above, is erroneous, thus, going
back on her own admission of the Petitioner-Respondent made in explicit
terms in paragraph 5 (a) and (b) of the statement of objections as enumerated
above and the 1st Respondent-Respondent upon her acquiescence of the said
findings of the learned High Court Judge as enumerated above.
Page 12 of 19
Hence, I would hold that the contention so advanced by the Petitioner-
Respondent and the 1st Respondent-Respondent cannot sustain in law and
therefore, it ought to be rejected as rightly, contended by the learned
President’s Counsel for the 2nd Respondent-Petitioner.
I would therefore, hold that the findings of the learned High Court Judge that
the affidavit in question is faulty, remains unchallenged and uncontroverted.
There now, remains for consideration only the question as to whether or not,
the defect in the affidavit of the Petitioner-Respondent filed along with her
petition under section 9 of the Act in support of the contents therein, is
curable in law as contended by the Petitioner-Respondent and the 1st
Respondent-Respondent or else, as to whether or not it is incurable in law as
contended by the 2nd Respondent-Petitioner.
It may now, be examined.
It was the position adverted to by the learned President’s Counsel for the 2nd
Respondent-Petitioner that a defect as such in an affidavit is one that would
go to the root of the action and therefore it is incurable and thus, be fatal to
the maintainability of the action and in the result, action should be dismissed
in-limine.
It was on the other hand, the position of both learned Senior State Counsel
for the Petitioner-Respondent as well as the learned President’s Counsel for
the 1st Respondent-Respondent that the defect is curable and therefore, it can
be cured by furnishing a fresh affidavit as directed by the learned High Court
Judge.
However, it is significant to observe that, both the Petitioner-Respondent as
well as the 1st Respondent-Respondent in the course of the argument before
us sought to contend further that, it is not a necessary requisite under the
summary procedure to attach by way of an exhibit, an affidavit to the written
petition presented to Court by the Petitioner under Chapter XXIV of the Civil
Procedure Code as amended, and therefore, non-attachment of an affidavit to
Page 13 of 19
the written petition or faulty affidavit attached thereto, will not affect the
validity of the application made thereunder, and therefore, the faulty affidavit
attached to the written petition will not vitiate the application or action
instituted under the summary procedure and as a result, the faulty affidavit
attached to the written petition filed in the High Court of the Province by the
Petitioner-Respondent will not vitiate the application and/or the action filed
thereat, under section 9 of the Act. On the other hand, it was contended by
the 2nd Respondent-Petitioner that it was a necessary requisite under the
summary procedure and non-compliance is fatal, and it would culminate in
the dismissal of the application and/or the action in-limine.
They may now, be examined.
With regard to the procedure to be adopted and followed in an action under
the Act, Section 9(2) thereof, provides that, “Every application under
subsection (1), shall be by way of summary procedure and shall be exempt
from the payment of any stamp duty under the Stamp Duty Act No. 43 of
Hence, in the instant action, the procedure to be adopted and followed as laid
down by section 9 of the Act, is the summary procedure as envisaged by
Chapter XXIV of the Civil Procedure as amended.
I would think it expedient at this juncture to examine the provisions of the
Civil Procedure Code as amended pertaining to the summary procedure.
Section 7 of the Civil Procedure as amended provides that,
“The procedure of an action may be either " regular " or " summary ".”.
Section 8 of the Civil Procedure as amended provides that,
“Save and except actions in which it is by this Ordinance or any other
law specially provided that proceedings may be taken by way of
summary procedure, every action shall commence and proceed by a
course of regular procedure, as hereinafter prescribed.”.
Page 14 of 19
Section 373 of the Civil Procedure as amended provides that,
“Every application to the Court, or action, of summary procedure shall
be instituted upon a duly stamped written petition presented to Court
by the applicant.”
Section 376 of the Civil Procedure as amended provides that,
“With the petition, and so far as conveniently can be attached thereto,
shall be exhibited such affidavits, authenticated copy records,
processes, or other documentary evidence as may be requisite to
furnish prima facie proof of the material facts set out or alleged in the
petition, or the court may in its discretion permit or direct the petitioner
to adduce oral evidence before the court for this purpose, which shall
be taken down by the court in writing.”
Section 377 of the Civil Procedure Code as amended provides that,
“If the court is satisfied on the evidence exhibited or adduced that the
material facts of the petition are prima facie established or is of opinion
that on the footing of these facts the petitioner is entitled to the remedy,
or to the order in his favour, for which the petition prays, or any part
thereof, then the court shall accordingly make either-
(a) an order nisi, conditioned to take effect in the event of the
respondent not showing cause against it on a day appointed by
the order for that purpose; or
(b) an interlocutory order appointing a day for the determination
of the matter of the petition, and intimating that the respondent
will be heard in opposition to the petition if he appears before the
court for that purpose on the day so appointed.”
Section 380 of the Civil Procedure Code as amended provides that,
Page 15 of 19
“If the court is not satisfied on the evidence exhibited or adduced that
the material facts of the petition are prima facie established or is of
opinion that on the footing of those facts the petitioner is not entitled to
the relief which he asks, then in either case the court shall refuse the
petition.”.
It is common ground that the instant action had been instituted by the
Petitioner-Respondent in the High Court of the Province under the summary
procedure as contained in chapter XXIV of the Civil Procedure Code as
amended, and as provided for by section 9 of the Act by presenting thereto, a
written petition as required by section 9(2) thereof, and hence, the application
of the Petitioner-Respondent is entirely, governed by the procedure laid down
by Chapter XXIV of the Civil Procedure Code as amended.
In the light of section 376 of the Civil Procedure Code as amended, it is a
mandatory requisite that with the Petition and so far as conveniently attached
thereto, shall be exhibited such affidavits, authenticated copy records,
processes, or other documentary evidence as may be requisite to furnish
prima facie proof of the material facts set out or alleged in the petition.
For; the affidavits, authenticated copy records, processes, or other
documentary evidence are the essential materials upon which the Court has
to be satisfied if the material facts of the petition are prima facie established
by the Petitioner. [Emphasis is mine]
What if, the affidavit attached to the petition is faulty or defective? Would the
dismissal of an action or application instituted under the summary
procedure, be automatic in such circumstances?
It may now, be examined.
It was inter-alia held by this Court in Damayanthi Abeywardene and
Another Vs. Hemalatha Abeywardene and others 1993 [1] SLR 272 at
page 277,
Page 16 of 19
“In terms of that section every application has to be made by way of
summary procedure and every person sought to be affected by the order
shall be named as a respondent in the petition. This leads us to a
consideration of the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code relating to
summary procedure. Section 376 states as follows :
“With the petition, and so far as conveniently can be
attached thereto,. shall be exhibited such affidavits,
authenticated copy records, processes, or other documentary
evidence as may be requisite to furnish prima facie proof of the
material facts set out or alleged in the petition, or the court may
in its discretion permit or direct the petitioner to adduce oral
evidence before the court for this purpose, which shall be taken
down by the court in writing”
It is to be seen from this section that a petition filed by way of
summary procedure should be supported by affidavits and other
documentary evidence necessary” to furnish prima facie proof of the
material facts set out or alleged in the petition.”. [Emphasis is mine]
In the light of the principle enunciated by this Court in the case in
Damayanthi Abeywardene and Another Vs. Hemalatha Abeywardene and
others (Supra), it is mandatory that, a petition filed by way of summary
procedure should be supported by affidavits and other documentary
evidence necessary, “to furnish prima facie proof of the material facts set out
or alleged in the petition.” [Emphasis is mine]
It was inter-alia, held by the Supreme Court in Gunaratne vs Translanka
Investments Ltd. and Another 1991 [2] SLR 1 at page 5 that, “Even in
applications of summary procedure, the Court has a discretion under section
376 to direct or permit the Petitioner to adduce oral evidence.”
Hence, the law as it stands now, as provided for by section 376 of the Civil
Procedure Code as amended and as enunciated by Supreme Court in
Gunaratne vs Translanka Investments Ltd. and Another (Supra) and by
Page 17 of 19
this Court in Damayanthi Abeywardene and Another Vs. Hemalatha
Abeywardene and others (Supra) is that it is mandatory that, a petition
filed by way of summary procedure should be supported by affidavits and
other documentary evidence necessary, “to furnish prima facie proof of the
material facts set out or alleged in the petition”, but, however, “Even in
applications of summary procedure, the Court has a discretion under
section 376 of the Civil Procedure Code as amended ‘to direct or permit’
the Petitioner to adduce oral evidence before the court necessary, “to
furnish prima facie proof of the material facts set out or alleged in the
petition” [Emphasis is mine]
The resultant position being that even though it is mandatory that, a petition
filed by way of summary procedure should be supported by affidavits and
other documentary evidence necessary, “to furnish prima facie proof of the
material facts set out or alleged in the petition”, but, however, “Even in
applications of summary procedure, the Court has a discretion under section
376 of the Civil Procedure Code as amended to direct or permit the Petitioner
to adduce oral evidence necessary, “to furnish prima facie proof of the
material facts set out or alleged in the petition” even in case, an affidavit
filed in support of the contents in the Petition presented to Court under the
summary procedure, is defective or faulty as in this case and hence, such a
defect in an affidavit is curable as provided for by section 376 of the Civil
Procedure Code as amended and as held by the Supreme Court in Gunaratne
vs Translanka Investments Ltd. and Another (Supra) [Emphasis is mine]
Hence, a defective and/or faulty affidavit filed in support of the contents in
the Petition presented to Court under the summary procedure, as in this case
is defective or faulty does not in any manner, give rise to an automatic
dismissal of an action or application instituted under the summary procedure
in Court for; defect as such is curable as enumerated above.
Even, in this instance too, the learned High Court Judge had ample power
under section 376 of the Civil Procedure Code as amended, to permit and/or
direct the Petitioner-Respondent to adduce oral evidence necessary, “to

furnish prima facie proof of the material facts set out or alleged in the
petition”, instead of directing the Petitioner-Respondent to furnish to Court
a duly, attested affidavit afresh.
However, I would find no provision under Chapter XXIV of the Civil Procedure
Code as amended which prevent the learned High Court Judge from directing
the Petitioner-Respondent to adduce oral evidence necessary, “to furnish
prima facie proof of the material facts set out or alleged in the petition”
in the event, he would find the affidavit filed along with the petition, defective
or faulty for one reason or the other as done in this instance by the learned
High Court Judge. [Emphasis is mine]
This brings me to the pivotal and material issue that had been advanced by
the learned President’s Counsel for the 2nd Respondent-Petitioner in the
course of the argument and it may now, be examined.
Record shows that, the learned High Court Judge had in his initial order dated
13.10.2025 (hereinafter called and referred to as “the initial order”), granted
the Petitioner-Respondent the relief as prayed for in prayer ‘a’, ‘b’ and ‘c’ of
the petition dated 03.10.2025 (A1).
Significance here is that, there’s nothing in his initial order to show on what
material he was satisfied that the material facts of the petition (A1) were prima
facie, established before he had made the initial order, granting the Petitioner-
Respondent the relief as prayed for in prayer ‘a’, ‘b’ and ‘c’ of the petition dated
03.10.2025 (A1) even though it would be essential and obligatory on the part
of the learned High Court Judge so to do, in view of the fact that, the learned
High Court Judge in the HC order (A10) had by implication, found the affidavit
of the Petitioner-Respondent filed along with her application (A1) under
summary procedure, defective or faculty. Nevertheless, the learned High
Court Judge had not opted even to disclose and/or specify in the subsequent
HC order (A10) on what material he was satisfied that the material facts of
the petition (A1) were prima facie, established before he had made order dated
Page 19 of 19
13.10.2025, granting the Petitioner-Respondent the relief as prayed for in
prayer ‘a’, ‘b’ and ‘c’ of the petition dated 03.10.2025 (A1).
In the circumstances, it clearly, and unequivocally, appears that the initial
order of the learned High Court Judge cannot sustain both in fact and law.
Hence, I would consider it highly, unsafe to permit the initial order to stand
any further.
I would thus, consider this to be a fit and proper case to exercise the extra-
ordinary revisionary jurisdiction vested in this Court by Article 138(1) of the
Constitution in order to avert grave miscarriage of justice thus, occurred.
Hence, I would acting in revision, set aside the initial order.
I would thus, direct the learned High Court Judge to hear and determine the
application of the Petitioner-Respondent afresh, on the strength of the duly,
attested affidavit that may be furnished to Court by the Petitioner-Respondent
as directed by the learned High Court Judge in the HC order (A10) and the
other material that were furnished to Court by the Petitioner-Respondent
along with her petition (A1) and conclude it as expeditiously, as possible
strictly, in accordance with the law as enumerated above affording it top
priority.
Subject to the above, I would allow the instant application in revision.
In view of all the above circumstances, I would make no order for costs.
